extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors / IP practitioners (especially those handling §101 rejections; includes software-related filings)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical prosecution strategies for drafting and amending patent applications and arguing before Examiners or on appeal to overcome rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (judicial exceptions/abstract idea). Emphasizes examiner-specific adaptation, claim amendment, appeal timing, and arguments focused on technical solutions, practical application, and pre-emption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the Supreme Court pre-emption policy (Alice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The concern driving the §101 exclusionary principle is pre-emption: distinguish patents that claim the 'building block[s]' of human ingenuity from those that integrate the building blocks into something more, thereby 'transform[ing]' them into a patent-eligible invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Alice v. CLS Bank: if a claim would 'risk disproportionately tying up the use of the underlying' ideas it is ineligible; if it integrates building blocks into something more it remains eligible. Use the pre-emption frame when crafting arguments that claims impose meaningful limits on the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt prosecution to the particular Examiner assigned
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Examiners vary in how they apply §101, tailor strategy to the Examiner on the case rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect information about the Examiner (allowance rate, average number of office actions, appeal statistics, case outcomes) and adapt claim amendment, argument style, and timing (e.g., appeal sooner against an Examiner with a very low allowance rate). Apply a multifaceted strategy to increase probability of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examiner metrics and case-history data to inform strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Before or during prosecution, use tools to get information about your Examiner: Allowance Rate (absolute and compared to the art unit); Average Number of Office Actions; Appeal Statistics; Outcomes in other cases the Examiner has worked on, and what strategies worked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Examiner statistics show low allowance rate or patterns of rejecting §101, consider earlier appeal or different amendment/argument tactics. Learn from other cases the Examiner handled to find arguments that succeeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for §101 rejections while drafting the application
rubrics_metrics.description: During initial drafting, identify technical problems and technical solutions, and draft the application with substantial technical details sourced from the inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly capture: (i) the technical problem; (ii) the technical solution; and (iii) substantial technical details that support the solution. Ensure these items come from the inventors so the specification supports later claim amendments and arguments about technical contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft the specification with substantial technical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical problem, technical solution, and technical details should be described with substantial technical detail in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial technical detail in the specification both supports claim amendments (adding technical limitations) and underpins arguments that the invention is rooted in technology rather than a mental or business method. Capture implementation details, data flows, algorithms, interfaces, hardware interactions, etc., as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amend claims during prosecution to add technical details
rubrics_metrics.description: During prosecution, amend the claims to add more technical details to avoid §101 rejections, while trying to preserve valuable scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding details is not trivial: balance the goal of overcoming §101 with client-value scope. Identify technical details that a plausible infringer would need; including such details is 'okay' when necessary for enforcement. Use claim drafting skill to maximize scope while inserting meaningful technical limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the appeal process at the right time
rubrics_metrics.description: If fighting §101 rejections through multiple office actions without success, consider appeal to the PTAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical triggers: third or fourth office action; earlier appeal may be warranted if Examiner has a particularly low allowance rate. Before appealing, ensure 'Are the claims in good shape?' and 'Are your arguments in good shape?'—i.e., fix claim language and prepare robust legal/technical arguments before appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require the Examiner to specify an alleged abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure the Examiner has actually identified an alleged abstract idea; challenge sloppy or vague characterizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners sometimes say things like 'these claims are similar to others that courts have determined are directed to abstract ideas' or treat each claim feature as a separate abstract idea. Force the Examiner to define the alleged abstract idea precisely so you can show how the claims are not directed to that abstract idea or how they meaningfully limit it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue claims incorporate the alleged 'abstract idea' into a practical application (impose a meaningful limit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are patent eligible if they 'use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the claimed invention integrates the alleged abstract idea into a practical application (e.g., produces a technical effect, requires particular technical steps or apparatus) and therefore imposes a meaningful limit. Use real examples where the claimed subject matter could not be rejected under §102/103 to bolster the meaningful-limit argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate that the claims cover only a tiny portion of the alleged abstract-idea universe
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the Examiner specifies an alleged abstract idea, show that your claims cover a tiny portion (or effectively zero) of that universe, indicating the claims do not pre-empt the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This directly captures the Supreme Court's pre-emption policy: if the claims occupy only a narrow slice of the abstract concept, they impose a meaningful limit. Note that not all Examiners accept this type of argument—be prepared with concrete technical distinctions and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue that the claimed subject matter cannot be performed in the human mind (technology-rootedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that the claimed invention cannot be performed in the human mind and is rooted in technology (as opposed to being a mere business method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions contrast business-method-like claims (often ineligible) with claims rooted in technology (eligible). Even Examiners who accept technology-based arguments often require the technology to be core to the invention (e.g., calling a server API to retrieve data may be a stronger technology showing than merely displaying data in a user interface). Use examples distinguishing core technical steps from high-level mental or managerial steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pragmatic: prune or avoid filings unlikely to succeed under §101
rubrics_metrics.description: By learning what works, practitioners can identify and prune cases that are less likely to succeed (or choose not to file them in the first place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize subject-matter areas (e.g., certain software inventions) where allowance is more difficult and allocate resources accordingly: either bolster the specification and claims to address §101 up front or decide not to file if the chances of overcoming §101 are too low relative to cost and client value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize subject-matter differences (software harder but possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowance is more difficult in certain subject matter areas (such as software), but strategic work can lead to success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat all technologies the same; focus on drafting and prosecution strategies that emphasize technical solutions and implementation details for software-related inventions to increase the chance of allowance.
